Chapter 6

Shipping Products and Code in Chaotic Environments

在混乱环境中交付产品与代码

We discussed in Chapter 1 that doing something is (almost) always better than doing nothing. We stand behind this take but acknowledge that it’s not very nuanced, because there is often more that you should or would do if you had the resources to. So, this means that you must decide what you will do and the order in which you will do it.

我们在第 1 章讨论过：做点什么几乎总是比什么都不做更好。我们仍然坚持这个观点，但也承认它不够细腻——因为如果手头有资源，你往往还有更多本应做、或本想做的事。这就意味着，你必须决定自己要做什么，以及按什么顺序去做。

To do this, you need to consider prioritization approaches and exactly how to determine your actions. However, circumstances in most chaotic situations don’t lend themselves to implementing highly structured processes and techniques. Indeed, applying those more elaborate processes in a chaotic environment often means serving the process instead of driving the outcome. Don’t underestimate the power of simplicity and common sense.

要做到这一点，你需要考虑优先级排序的方法，以及究竟该如何确定自己的行动。然而，大多数混乱局面的环境并不适合套用高度结构化的流程与技巧。事实上，在混乱环境里硬塞那些繁复的流程，往往意味着你在侍奉流程本身，而不是在推动结果。不要低估简单与常识的力量。

We need to find some techniques that meet the following criteria:

我们需要找一些满足以下标准的技巧：

  • Inspire confidence.

    激发信心。

  • Be execution-focused.

    以执行为中心。

  • Be lightweight and adaptable.

    轻量且可调整。

  • Foster continuous learning.

    促进持续学习。

  • Focus on communication and collaboration.

    聚焦沟通与协作。

In this chapter, we explore what this means and introduce you to some approaches that could either meet your needs or be adapted to meet them.

在本章中，我们会探讨这些标准意味着什么，并向你介绍一些方法——它们要么直接满足你的需求，要么稍作调整即可满足。

— 原书第 113 页 —

Note

提示

This won’t be a detailed guide to prioritization and the software development lifecycle (SDLC). But it does offer a crash course designed to equip you with the skills to manage right now. For deeper guides, check out Martin Fowler’s collection of Agile guides and Atlassian’s SDLC guide.

本章不会是一份关于优先级排序和软件开发生命周期（SDLC）的详尽指南。但它提供了一门速成课，旨在让你立刻具备上手管理所需的技能。想要更深入的指南，可以参考 Martin Fowler 的 Agile 指南文集，以及 Atlassian 的 SDLC 指南。

Inspire Confidence

激发信心

You need to make your team confident that processes will work most of the time; here, we’re fond of the 80/20 rule: if a process works 80% of the time, it’s a success. Additionally, every successful process iteration will give the team more confidence and reassurance that they are improving. Growing confidence, or at least not eroding it, is also achieved through admitting that processes can be failures—and making those failures learning opportunities.

你需要让团队相信：流程在大多数情况下是管用的。这里我们很推崇 80/20 法则——一个流程只要在 80% 的时候管用，就算成功。此外，每一次成功的流程迭代都会让团队更有信心，更确信自己在进步。要让信心增长（或至少不被消磨），还要敢于承认流程也可能失败——并把这些失败转化为学习机会。

Here, you can also start small and build up. For example, in many chaotic environments, estimation is a scary prospect. The question of how long something will take—especially if those estimates are being communicated to leadership or other teams—often results in much debate and churn. You will inevitably get those initial estimates wrong. When that happens, the team will likely lose confidence in their ability to deliver and in your ability to lead.

在这一点上，你同样可以从小处着手、逐步建立。例如，在很多混乱环境里，估算是一件让人发怵的事。一件事要做多久——尤其是当这些估算要汇报给领导层或其他团队时——往往会引发大量争论和反复折腾。你几乎必然会把最初的估算搞错。一旦如此，团队很可能会对自己的交付能力、以及对你的领导能力失去信心。

Instead of only making a wild guess, acknowledge uncertainty and then put a stake in the ground. For example, you could adjust your initial tolerance to accept a 50% variance in an estimate: if your team thinks it’s a week of effort, it could be two weeks. It’s still a guess, but you acknowledge that you don’t know what you don’t know. Admitting uncertainty and articulating an approach to add more rigor and help reduce that uncertainty is much more confidence-inspiring than throwing arbitrary estimates out. This also drives a desire to learn, measure, and refine the process, hopefully reducing that variation over time as you gain experience.

与其胡乱猜一个数，不如先承认不确定性，再立下一个基准。例如，你可以把最初的容错度放宽到接受估算有 50% 的偏差：如果团队认为要做一周，那它也可能是两周。这仍然是猜测，但你承认了自己有所不知。承认不确定性、并讲清楚打算如何增加严谨性、逐步缩小这种不确定性，比随手扔出一个拍脑袋的估算要能建立得多的信心。这也会激发学习、度量和改进流程的意愿，希望随着经验积累，这种偏差会逐渐缩小。

In chaotic environments, you want to instill confidence and reduce fear. The best way to do this is to have quick, iterative wins that grow your and the team’s confidence. In a prior role, James inherited an engineering organization stuck in a cycle of constantly changing priorities, incidents, and temporary fixes. To counteract this situation, the team had stacked processes onto their lifecycle to gain some control of the problem. As a result, the whole software development process had ground to a halt. James stripped away the process to address this and started looking at what mattered to this team at their current level of maturity: shipping quality code. After some initial shock, the team began to ship code. The mere experience of moving forward and delivering gave the team enormous levels of confidence. The code was far from perfect, but the forward progress—after months of stagnation—changed the whole mental outlook of the team.

在混乱环境中，你要做的是注入信心、减少恐惧。最好的办法，是用快速、迭代的小胜来不断增长你和团队的信心。James 在之前的一个岗位上，接手过一个陷入恶性循环的工程组织：优先级天天变、事故不断、临时打补丁。为了控制局面，团队在开发生命周期上层层叠加流程。结果是，整个软件开发过程彻底停摆。James 做的是把这些流程剥掉，转而关注在团队当前成熟度下真正重要的事：交付高质量代码。一开始团队有些不适应，但很快就开始发布代码了。光是“往前推进、真正交付”这件事本身，就给了团队巨大的信心。代码远非完美，但在停滞数月之后，这种向前的进展彻底改变了团队的精神面貌。

We can return to April at PixelCurl as an example of how this might pan out.

我们可以回到 PixelCurl 的 April 这个例子，看看这一切是如何展开的。

— 原书第 114 页 —

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

Similarly, April at PixelCurl faced a confidence crisis with the StudioOps team. Senior engineers working in silos had created an environment where junior engineers felt unsupported and isolated. April’s first priority wasn’t to add complex processes but to rebuild confidence through small wins. She started by pairing senior and junior engineers on a quick bug-fix sprint—nothing revolutionary, just getting people to ship code together. The shared success of clearing a backlog that had been lingering for months gave both groups a confidence boost and helped rebuild collaboration between senior and junior engineers.

类似地，PixelCurl 的 April 也面临 StudioOps 团队的信心危机。高级工程师各自为战，营造出一种让初级工程师感到孤立无援的环境。April 的首要任务不是叠加复杂流程，而是通过小胜重建信心。她先是让高级和初级工程师结对，一起参加一个快速修 bug 的冲刺——没什么革命性的东西，只是让大家一起把代码发出去。他们共同清掉了积压数月的待办，这次共享的胜利让两类人都重拾信心，也重建了高、初级工程师之间的协作。

Importantly, you must also acknowledge your losses and turn them into learning and improvement opportunities. Confidence comes from knowing there is direction—that someone has a plan and is at least trying to drive improvements. Grandiose promises and complex frameworks rarely achieve the same result.

重要的是，你也必须承认自己的失败，并把它们转化为学习和改进的机会。信心来自于“知道有方向”——有人有计划、并且至少在努力推动改进。空口大话和复杂框架，很少能带来同样的效果。

Be Execution-Focused

以执行为中心

We must also ensure our chosen processes focus on execution and outcomes. Any process that prioritizes the outcome in favor of the process is a red flag—for example, when conducting a ceremony becomes more important than actually shipping the product, or worse, when teams spend time arguing over or endlessly fine-tuning processes. There’s a specific type of person—usually the one who reads the rules intensely when playing a board game—who lives to create processes and, more dangerously, to identify every possible edge case and insist the process must address them. Other people cling to process as an anchor amid the chaos around them or as a way to mitigate risk.

我们还必须确保所选流程聚焦于执行和结果。任何让流程凌驾于结果之上的做法都是一个危险信号——例如，把“开会走仪式”看得比真正交付产品还重要；更糟的是，团队把时间花在争论流程、或无休止地微调流程上。有这么一类人（通常就是玩桌游时死抠规则的那种人），他们活着就是为了造流程，更危险的是，他们还非要找出每一个可能的边界情况，并坚持流程必须把它们都覆盖到。另一些人则把流程当作混乱中的一根锚，或当作一种缓释风险的手段。

As leaders, we and our teams are all ultimately measured by deliverables, and we must keep that in sight in every task we undertake. “We built a comprehensive process that addressed every edge case” is meaningless unless the process results in a successful deliverable. The same goes for “the process worked”—if it didn’t achieve the deliverable, it didn’t work. We like to approach process design from the perspective of the deliverable and work backward from there. We know what we want as a deliverable—for example, shipping a release, a product iteration, or delivering a feature—and then layer in the bare minimum process necessary to help the team achieve it. In “Prioritization Techniques” on page 101, we explain how to build those layers, and we provide examples and models designed to be execution-focused.

作为领导者，我们和团队最终都是靠交付物来被衡量的，在做每一件事时都必须把这一点放在眼里。“我们建了一套覆盖所有边界情况的完备流程”——如果这套流程没有带来成功的交付，这句话毫无意义。“流程运转良好”也一样——如果它没带来交付物，它就没运转良好。我们喜欢从交付物出发来设计流程，然后倒推：我们先想清楚想要的交付物是什么——比如发布一个版本、一次产品迭代、或交付一个功能——再叠加帮助团队达成它所需的最低限度的流程。在第 101 页的“优先级排序技巧”一节中，我们会解释如何层层叠加这些流程，并给出以执行为中心的示例与模型。

— 原书第 115 页 —

Be Lightweight and Adaptable

轻量且可调整

This leads us to the importance of choosing lightweight processes. One of our favorite maxims is: You can always add a process, but it’s much harder to remove it. So, we always start with the bare minimum of process necessary to execute. We focus on guardrails to ensure the team is focused on what needs to be done and executing on that. Your mission in building the process is to provide those guardrails and the resources necessary to execute, and to help remove any friction or obstacles in the way of that execution. This mission is much easier if you let the process grow from a seedling rather than attempting to plant a forest.

这就引出了选择轻量流程的重要性。我们很喜欢一句格言：流程随时可以加，但要删掉它就难多了。因此，我们总是从执行所需的最低限度流程起步。我们聚焦于“护栏”，确保团队专注于该做的事并把它做掉。你建流程的使命，是提供这些护栏和执行所需的资源，并帮助清除执行路上的摩擦与障碍。如果你让流程从一棵小苗慢慢长起来，而不是一上来就想种出一片森林，这个使命会轻松得多。

Kevin Stewart, an engineering leader at several startups, paraphrases Michael Pollan’s Food Rules to describe what that process should look like.

曾在多家初创公司担任工程领导的 Kevin Stewart，改写了 Michael Pollan 的《食物的法则》（Food Rules），来描述流程应当是什么样子：

Michael Pollan’s food rules:
    Eat food.
    Not too much.
    Mostly plants.

Become:
    Use a process.
    Not too much.
    Mostly agile.

Let’s break down these rules. First, use a process: you must have something. Many early-stage companies are collections of individual contributors working separately on a product. If you’re working with a few smart engineers building a minimum viable product (MVP) with a narrow focus or an obvious set of objectives or features, this approach often works—sometimes even moderately well. It also works when two to four folks sit around a table in a coworking space. However, it doesn’t work if you need to make decisions at a larger scale about what is a priority. And it doesn’t work as you scale the size of a team or company or if you need to collaborate with other people or teams. Your role is to build up your team’s capacity, capability, and confidence. To do that, you’ll need to establish a few simple structures.

我们来拆解这几条法则。第一，要用流程：你必须得有个东西。很多早期公司就是一群各自为战的个体贡献者，各自在产品上做自己的事。如果你面对的是几个聪明工程师，在做一个聚焦明确、目标或功能显而易见的最小可行产品（MVP），这种做法往往行得通——有时甚至还挺不错。当只有两三个人在联合办公空间围桌而坐时，它也管用。但是，当你需要在更大范围内决定“什么才是优先级”时，它就不管用了。当团队或公司规模扩大、或你需要与其他人或团队协作时，它也不管用。你的职责是建立团队的产能、能力和信心。要做到这一点，你需要建立几个简单的结构。

Secondly: not too much. We’ve discussed why this is important. Too much process leads people to serve the process rather than deliver the outcome.

第二点：不要太多。我们已经讨论过这为什么重要。流程太多，会让人去侍奉流程本身，而不是交付结果。

— 原书第 116 页 —

Thirdly: mostly agile. You’ll note the “mostly,” and that “agile” here is not capitalized. That’s a deliberate decision by Stewart. It’s important to highlight that the term agile (or Agile) now encompasses an extensive variety of practices and disciplines. Some are simple, lightweight processes, and others are multipage volumes that make the assembly instructions for a Lego Death Star™ look simple. However, we still want to choose some principles, practices, and processes from the Agile ecosystem.

第三点：大部分用敏捷（mostly agile）。你会注意到“大部分”这个词，也会注意到这里的 agile 没有大写。这是 Stewart 刻意的决定。需要强调的是，agile（或 Agile）这个词如今已经涵盖了极其庞杂的一整套实践与方法论。其中一些是简单、轻量的流程，另一些则是动辄几十页的大部头——相比之下，连乐高死星（Death Star™）的组装说明书都显得简单了。尽管如此，我们仍然希望从敏捷生态中挑选一些原则、实践和流程来用。

There is a more metaphysical question that many ask at this point: why Agile at all? You could argue a lot of perspectives here; there’s extensive data and analysis of the success and failure of various Agile processes, but we like to summarize it as “the least bad approach to building products.” (We discuss other frameworks for problems outside of product development later in the chapter.) That might appear oversimplified, so let’s fill in some blanks. First, the original Agile Manifesto is over 20 years old; there has been lots of movement since then. Second, consider the work of the original manifesto authors:

很多人在这一步会问一个更形而上的问题：到底为什么要用敏捷？这个问题可以从很多角度争论；关于各种敏捷流程的成败，已经有大量数据和分析，但我们喜欢把它概括为“构建产品时最不差的那种方式”。（本章后面会讨论产品开发之外问题所适用的其他框架。）这听起来可能过于简化，我们来补几句。首先，最初的《敏捷宣言》已经 20 多年了，这些年里发生了很多变化。其次，看看宣言原作者们写下的东西：

We are uncovering better ways of developing software by doing it and helping others do it. Through this work, we have come to value:

我们正在通过亲身实践、并帮助他人实践，来探寻更好的软件开发方式。经由这项工作，我们逐渐重视：

  • Individuals and interactions over processes and tools

    个体与互动，高于流程与工具

  • Working software over comprehensive documentation

    可工作的软件，高于详尽的文档

  • Customer collaboration over contract negotiation

    客户协作，高于合同谈判

  • Responding to change over following a plan

    响应变化，高于遵循计划

That is, while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more.

也就是说，尽管右列各项也有其价值，但我们更看重左列各项。

Some of that might sound familiar to anyone who has gotten this far into the book. We believe in many of the same values articulated in the manifesto. The final line is especially resonant because its interpretation has driven much of the change in and adaptation of Agile over the years. The relative value placed on the right and left items often shapes the specific Agile approaches to building software. But we’ve also built software under less-than-ideal circumstances in chaotic environments, so we apply some pragmatism to the manifesto’s values and the weights applied to each side. That’s where “mostly agile” comes into play. Rather than dogmatically choosing to “do Agile,” selectively adopt the practices that work for you and your team, apply them, and put aside the rest; you may find some useful later. The real power of agile isn’t in following every ceremony to the letter, it’s in embracing its core principles of people, shipping software, collaboration, flexibility, and responsiveness. This is especially true in chaotic environments where you need to inspire confidence in your team, adapt to rapidly changing circumstances, and make decisions without perfect information.

读到这里的读者，对其中一些话大概会觉得耳熟。我们认同宣言里阐述的许多价值观。最后那句话尤其令人共鸣，因为多年来敏捷的演变与适配，很大程度上正是由对这句话的解读推动的。对左右两列各自权重的取舍，往往决定了构建软件时具体采用哪种敏捷做法。但我们也曾在混乱环境里、在并不理想的条件下构建过软件，因此我们对宣言的价值观、以及两侧权重的分配，采取了一定的实用主义态度。这正是“大部分敏捷”的用武之地：不要教条地“做敏捷”，而是有选择地采用对你和团队管用的实践，用起来，其余的先放到一边——以后说不定哪天又有用。敏捷真正的力量，不在于逐字逐句地走完每一场仪式，而在于拥抱它的核心原则：人、交付软件、协作、灵活、响应变化。在混乱环境中尤其如此——你需要给团队注入信心、适应瞬息万变的局势，并在信息并不完备时做出决策。

— 原书第 117 页 —

We’re not going to explain Agile development in any significant depth, as there are a lot of resources out there that can do that for you. Some good starting points are:

我们不打算深入讲解敏捷开发，因为市面上已经有大量资料可以替你做这件事。一些不错的起点包括：

  • Martin Fowler’s collection of Agile guides

    Martin Fowler 的敏捷指南文集

  • The Art of Agile Development by James Shore and Shane Warden

    James Shore 与 Shane Warden 合著的《敏捷开发的艺术》

  • Essential Scrum: A Practical Guide to the Most Popular Agile Process by Kenneth S. Rubin

    Kenneth S. Rubin 的《Scrum 精髓：最流行敏捷实践实战指南》

  • User Stories Applied: For Agile Software Development by Mike Cohn

    Mike Cohn 的《用户故事与敏捷方法》

We will, however, express our opinions about what bits of Agile work and how to configure them in chaotic environments. We continue to emphasize the importance of experimenting and finding a process model and cadence that works for you and your team.

但我们会就敏捷中哪些部分管用、以及在混乱环境中如何配置它们，给出我们自己的看法。我们始终强调：要去试验，找到一套对你和团队真正管用的流程模型和节奏。

Choosing the right pieces and level of process also helps you drive the iterative development of how your team ships software. Lightweight, simple, and adaptable processes lend themselves to experimentation and continuous improvement. If you try something new as an experiment, but it doesn’t work, then you can iterate to something new and try that until you find the process that fits, or so that you can scale your process as your team grows in confidence, capacity, and capability.

选对流程的组成部分和轻重程度，也能帮助你推动团队交付软件方式的迭代演进。轻量、简单、可调整的流程，天然适合试验和持续改进。如果你把某个新做法当作一次试验来试，结果不管用，那就可以再迭代到新做法、再试，直到找到合适的流程；或者随着团队在信心、产能和能力上的成长，逐步扩展你的流程。

Foster Continuous Learning

促进持续学习

Any new process is a learning opportunity. When you implement a new process, think about a way to measure its efficiency and efficacy. Implementing a process without the means to measure it is a wasted opportunity. Those measures can be qualitative or quantitative (or both). In the agile world, a qualitative measure could be a retrospective, the team’s state of mind, while a quantitative measure could be the percentage of stories completed in a sprint against the plan. In exploring potential methods, we highlight how each can be measured and what to take from those results.

任何新流程都是一次学习机会。当你推行一个新流程时，就要想清楚如何度量它的效率和效果。推行一个流程却没有度量它的手段，就是浪费了一次机会。这些度量可以是定性的，也可以是定量的（或者两者兼有）。在敏捷的世界里，定性度量可以是一次回顾会、团队的心态状态；定量度量可以是一个冲刺中实际完成的故事数相对计划的百分比。在探讨各种方法时，我们会着重说明每种方法如何度量、以及该从结果中读出什么。

Measurement also supports experimentation. We need to be adaptable and flexible. Running measurable experiments in process provides comfort that we’re making the best possible decisions, or at least decisions supported by data. So, collect feedback, measure outcomes, and refine processes over time.

度量也支撑试验。我们需要具备适应性和灵活性。在流程上跑可度量的试验，能让我们安心——我们做的是尽可能好的决策，或者至少是有数据支撑的决策。因此，要收集反馈、度量结果，并随时间不断改进流程。

Focus on Communication and Collaboration

聚焦沟通与协作

Remember that new or altered processes are changes. And change is scary for people, especially when it’s change tied to how we do our work. Best practices to ensure people feel more comfortable with change include:

请记住：新流程或被改动的流程本身就是一种变革。而变革对人来说是可怕的，尤其是当这种变革与我们的工作方式直接相关时。要让人们更安心地接受变革，最佳做法包括：

— 原书第 118 页 —

  • Open, transparent communication

    开放、透明的沟通

  • Collaboration

    协作

  • Not doing too much at once

    不要一次铺得太多

It’s crucial to communicate changes to your team. Keep your team informed of the progress of the process and any proposed changes. Be transparent and honest with them about the challenges you are facing, what’s going well, and what’s not. Odds are that they already know what’s working and what’s not, so making any measurements, challenges, and success transparent to them grows their trust and confidence in you. Build process methodically; introducing too much at once will mean people will feel overwhelmed. So start small.

把变革沟通给你的团队至关重要。让团队随时了解流程的进展、以及任何拟议中的改动。对他们透明、诚实地讲清楚：你正面临哪些挑战、哪些做得不错、哪些不行。很可能他们本来就知道什么管用、什么不管用，因此把度量结果、面临的挑战和取得的成绩都对他们透明，会增进他们对你的信任和信心。有条不紊地建流程；一次推太多，人们会被压垮。所以，从小处开始。

When you’re building processes, remember that you are not the only person affected by them, and you’re also not likely to be the one executing them every day. Go to the source and work directly with your team to find processes that work for them and you. The people running the process daily often have valuable insight into opportunities and challenges, and involving the team in developing the process will increase their sense of ownership, control, and confidence in it.

在搭建流程时，请记住：你不是唯一受它影响的人，而且你大概率也不是那个每天执行它的人。走到一线去，直接和你的团队一起，找出对他们和你都管用的流程。每天执行流程的人，往往对其中的机会和挑战有宝贵的洞察；让团队参与流程的制定，会增强他们对流程的主人翁感、掌控感和信心。

Celebrate

庆祝

Remember to celebrate your successes. As much as we focus on improvement, iteration, and turning failures into opportunities, we should also acknowledge when things go well. If you have a successful week or sprint outcome—no matter how small—acknowledge it and celebrate it. Confidence in a new or changed process is fragile, especially in chaotic and unpredictable environments. So, bolster that confidence by recognizing when your team is successful.

别忘了庆祝你们的成功。尽管我们如此强调改进、迭代、把失败转化为机会，但我们也应当在事情顺利时给予肯定。如果你有了成功的一周或一个冲刺成果——无论多小——都要承认它、庆祝它。对新流程或改动后流程的信心是脆弱的，尤其在混乱、不可预测的环境里。因此，当团队取得成功时，要通过认可来加固这份信心。

Other Prioritization Concerns

其他优先级考量

Additionally, we have three further concerns when considering prioritization approaches:

此外，在考虑优先级排序方法时，我们还有另外三点顾虑：

  • Not all work is created equal.

    并非所有工作生而平等。

  • Not all work can use the same process.

    并非所有工作都能用同一套流程。

  • Not all work is known at the start of prioritization.

    并非所有工作在排序之初就已明朗。

— 原书第 119 页 —

Not All Work Is Created Equal

并非所有工作生而平等

What do we mean by saying that not all work is created equal? Prioritization is rarely single threaded; your team will likely do many different things. Seldom can you produce a stack-ranked queue of work that your team must do. Work comes in various sizes and has different skill requirements, dependencies, and difficulty levels. When thinking about scheduling work for my teams, we think more about working on a jigsaw puzzle than imagining it as a queue: what fits where, with what else, with whom, and in what order. We need to select processes that cater to this variation without requiring enormous overhead—both people and operational overheads—to track them. Indeed, as we’ve discussed when we talked about the myriad roles you might need to adopt, you and your team will likely be the program and project (and sometimes product) managers for most of the work you’re undertaking.

说“并非所有工作生而平等”是什么意思？优先级排序很少是单线程的；你的团队很可能要同时做好几件不同的事。你很少能拉出一条严格排序的队列，让团队照着做就行。工作大小不一，所需技能、依赖关系和难度也各不相同。在为团队安排工作时，我们更多是把它看作拼拼图，而不是排队列：哪块放在哪里、和哪块拼在一起、由谁来拼、按什么顺序拼。我们需要选择能适配这种多样性的流程，而又不必为了追踪它们付出巨大的开销——无论是人力还是运营开销。事实上，正如我们在讨论你可能需要扮演的种种角色时说过的，对于你承担的大部分工作，你和团队很可能同时兼任项目集经理、项目经理（有时还是产品经理）。

Not All Work Can Use the Same Process

并非所有工作都能用同一套流程

Many people try to apply a uniform methodology to every task they undertake. We often see this in organizations that adopt some variant of Agile methodologies. Agile is well suited to smaller iterative tasks, but some projects don’t fit this approach. For example, moving an office lends itself much more to traditional project management methodologies, as they can have complex dependencies and very linear timelines. There is often an inherent skepticism about the efficacy of waterfall-style projects—and in our opinion, rightly so when considering building software products. However, for some projects, like an office move, traditional project management can be the right choice, and you should have the ability to plan and manage a project like this effectively.

很多人试图把同一套方法论套用到手头的每一项任务上。我们常常在采用某种敏捷变体的组织里看到这种现象。敏捷很适合较小的、迭代式的任务，但有些项目并不适合这种做法。例如，办公室搬迁就更适合传统项目管理方法，因为这类项目可能有复杂的依赖关系和非常线性的时间线。人们对瀑布式项目的有效性往往天生抱有怀疑——我们也同意，在构建软件产品时确实如此。但对于办公室搬迁这类项目，传统项目管理可能才是正确选择，而你应当具备有效规划和管理这类项目的能力。

Not All Work Is Known at the Start of Prioritization

并非所有工作在排序之初就已明朗

A common analogy for describing new or changed work that appears after the project starts is: building the plane while it’s in flight. James is not a good flyer, so he does not enjoy this analogy. It also galls him because most of the time, none of us are building airplanes, whose design and construction—some recent examples aside—have considerably higher tolerances and standards than creating a marketing website. But the point is that the reality of many chaotic environments is constant change and evolution.

描述项目开始后才冒出来的新工作或变更工作，有一个常用比方：在飞机飞行途中造飞机。James 不太会坐飞机，所以他不喜欢这个比方。而且这让他恼火，因为大多数时候我们谁也不是在造飞机——飞机的设计与建造（撇开最近的一些例子不谈）在容错和标准上，远比做一个营销网站要严苛得多。但这个比方的要点在于：许多混乱环境的现实，就是持续不断的变化与演进。

— 原书第 120 页 —

Many leaders, especially those from larger organizations, need help in chaotic environments because they expect the same support structures—like a prioritization framework or a project management methodology—to be in place. In a chaotic environment, you’re not just working within these structures but building them. We need to ensure our processes are:

许多领导者，尤其是来自大组织的领导者，在混乱环境里需要帮助，因为他们以为那些支撑性结构——比如优先级框架、项目管理方法论——已经现成摆在那里。在混乱环境里，你不仅是在这些结构之中工作，更是在亲手建造它们。我们需要确保自己的流程：

  • Flexible enough to accommodate change

    足够灵活，能够容纳变化

  • Strong enough to protect against fluctuating priorities

    足够稳固，能够抵御优先级的反复横跳

This balancing act is often a lot harder than it looks. Later in the chapter, we discuss some techniques to help you strike a balance between these, ensuring that you execute and deliver what is required of you and your team, rather than being mired in an endless bog of changed priorities.

这种平衡往往比看起来难得多。本章后面会讨论一些技巧，帮你在两者之间取得平衡，确保你执行并交付组织要求于你和团队的东西，而不是深陷在优先级不断变更的无底泥潭里。

Prioritization Techniques

优先级排序技巧

We’ve established that in chaotic and rapidly changing environments, you must prioritize and balance your work to ensure that you’re working on the right things in the right combination and sequence. Getting this right helps engineering leaders make informed decisions and deliver your organization’s needs. Now, let’s delve into the approach we propose for prioritizing software and product development and how it can help you balance work effectively.

我们已经明确：在混乱、快速变化的环境中，你必须对工作排优先级、加以平衡，确保你在以正确的组合和顺序做正确的事。把这件事做对，能帮助工程领导者做出有依据的决策，交付组织所需。现在，我们来深入讲讲我们推荐的软件与产品开发优先级排序方法，以及它如何帮你有效地平衡工作。

First, consider some of the inputs you should evaluate when prioritizing tasks.

首先，看看在给任务排优先级时，你应当评估哪些输入项。

Key Inputs for Decision Making

决策的关键输入

Making good prioritization decisions does require some base information—not perfect information, but some initial understanding of why you are doing the work, its impact, and a broad understanding of any requirements. More information is better, but this isn’t always available or complete. When it comes to prioritizing work, several critical factors should guide your decision-making process:

做出好的优先级决策，确实需要一些基础信息——不必是完美信息，但要对“为什么做这件事、它有什么影响、需求大致是什么”有个初步认识。信息越多越好，但信息并不总是现成或完整的。在给工作排优先级时，有几个关键因素应当指引你的决策过程：

— 原书第 121 页 —

Business impact

业务影响

Evaluate how each task contributes to the product’s or organization’s goals, or both. Does it drive revenue, enhance customer satisfaction, or open new market opportunities? Tasks with a higher business impact typically deserve higher priority.

评估每项任务对产品目标或组织目标（或两者）的贡献。它能否带来收入、提升客户满意度、或打开新的市场机会？业务影响更高的任务，通常值得更高的优先级。

Urgency

紧迫性

Consider each task’s time sensitivity. Are there deadlines imposed by go-to-market needs, contractual obligations, or competitive pressures? Urgent tasks need to be addressed promptly to avoid negative consequences.

考虑每项任务对时间的敏感程度。是否有由上市需求、合同义务或竞争压力带来的截止日期？紧急任务需要及时处理，以免造成负面后果。

Effort

工作量

How much effort is required to complete the task. Is it days, weeks, or months? You need to understand if a task requires more capacity than you have, or if its timeline will create issues that clash with the business impact or urgency.

完成这项任务需要投入多少努力。是几天、几周还是几个月？你需要判断：一项任务所需的产能是否超出了你拥有的产能，或者它的时间线是否会造成与业务影响或紧迫性相冲突的问题。

People

人员

Assess your team members’ availability and skill sets. Do you have the people to execute the tasks efficiently, and do those people have the right skills?

评估团队成员的可用度和技能组合。你是否有能高效执行这些任务的人？这些人是否具备合适的技能？

Dependencies

依赖关系

Identify interdependencies between tasks. Some tasks can begin only after others are completed. This is common sense in most cases, especially for product development. However, other projects—such as moving an office or a complex deployment—may require a clearer understanding of the sequence of tasks.

识别任务之间的相互依赖。有些任务必须等别的任务完成后才能开始。这在大多数情况下是常识，尤其在产品开发中。但另一些项目——比如办公室搬迁或一次复杂的部署——可能需要更清楚地理清任务的先后顺序。

We don’t generally create separate systems for storing this information; we use existing tools and frameworks that include this scope in their remit.

我们一般不会为存储这些信息另建一套系统；我们使用那些职责范围本就涵盖这些内容的现有工具和框架。

Utilize Established Frameworks

利用成熟框架

Just as we consider agile a broad foundation for guiding how we operate, we also leverage established frameworks—in part or whole—when choosing how to prioritize work. These tools provide structured approaches to assess and rank tasks or features based on specific criteria. There are a lot of existing frameworks that you can draw upon to bootstrap prioritization, and many frameworks are already supported in tools like ticketing systems.

正如我们把敏捷当作指导行事方式的广泛基础一样，在选择如何给工作排优先级时，我们也会利用成熟框架——或借用一部分，或整体采用。这些工具提供了结构化的方法，按特定标准来评估和排序任务或功能。有大量现成框架可供你拿来为优先级排序搭起起步框架，而且许多框架已经被工单系统等工具内置支持。

Like agile, we’re not dogmatic about our choices or usage of these frameworks; we take the bits that work—sometimes from several frameworks—and shape them into a system that works for us and meets our objectives and constraints, especially the need to be flexible and adaptable.

和敏捷一样，我们在这些框架的选择和使用上也不教条；我们拿走管用的部分——有时同时从好几个框架里拿——把它们塑造成一套适合我们、能满足我们目标与约束的系统，尤其是灵活可调整这一需求。

As the base of our approach, we start with one of the classic techniques for understanding work: the user story.

作为我们方法的基础，我们从理解工作的经典技巧之一开始：用户故事（user story）。

— 原书第 122 页 —

Tools of the Trade

趁手工具

You should find a tool to manage your prioritization, workload, and backlog. There are a lot of potential tools out there that can help, ranging from spreadsheets to Trello, right up to complex Agile management tools like Linear, Shortcut, and Jira (and a dozen others). We don’t have a strong opinion on choosing a specific tool. Try a few out and see what works for you and your team. Different tools also have different audiences. A tool like Jira, for example, has an extensive collection of features and integrations that may be overwhelming to a small team (and hard to manage), so a more straightforward tool might be the better choice. Additionally, you might evolve through several iterations of tools as your needs change.

你应当找一个工具来管理优先级、工作量和待办清单。市面上能帮忙的工具很多：从电子表格到 Trello，再到 Linear、Shortcut、Jira（以及其他十几种）这类复杂的敏捷管理工具。我们对选哪个具体工具没有强烈偏好。多试几个，看哪个对你和团队管用。不同工具面向不同的用户群。例如 Jira 这类工具，功能和集成极其丰富，对小团队来说可能不堪重负（也难以管理），这时一个更简单直接的工具可能是更好的选择。此外，随着需求变化，你可能会历经好几代工具的迭代。

User stories

用户故事

User stories center around mapping the user journey to visualize features based on user needs. It’s a straightforward concept: imagine (or ask the customer) how they will use your product or a specific feature. The user story approach focuses on delivering an MVP that satisfies core user requirements, enabling you to provide value early on. While user stories are more of a product decomposition method rather than a prioritization technique in their own right, we think your prioritization technique needs to have inputs that maximize your ability to prioritize effectively. User stories are those inputs. Good user stories also encourage efficient use of your people, focusing on high-impact features (more on this shortly). They also encourage addressing high-risk items earlier, potentially reducing future issues. Finally, aligning development with customer needs often correlates with your business objectives.

用户故事的核心，是把用户旅程映射出来，基于用户需求来可视化功能。这个概念很简单：设想（或直接问客户）他们会怎样使用你的产品或某个具体功能。用户故事方法聚焦于交付一个能满足核心用户需求的 MVP，让你尽早提供价值。用户故事本身更像是一种产品分解方法，而不是一种独立的优先级排序技巧，但我们认为，你的排序技巧需要有一些输入项，来最大化你有效排序的能力——用户故事就是这些输入项。好的用户故事还能鼓励高效用人，把注意力放在高影响的功能上（稍后详述）。它们也鼓励更早处理高风险项，从而有可能减少未来的问题。最后，让开发与客户需求对齐，往往也和你的业务目标相吻合。

We like user stories because they encourage and reinforce iterative development and continuous product refinement based on feedback and (optimally) data-driven insights. It emphasizes understanding the user’s perspective, ensuring that development efforts align with user expectations and needs. You’ve likely seen user stories applied to product development—for example, “you’re building a customer-facing product.” However, we think they equally apply to other purposes, including internal tools and platforms. Like customer-facing products, those areas have users too.

我们喜欢用户故事，因为它鼓励并强化迭代开发，以及基于反馈（最好是数据驱动的洞察）持续打磨产品。它强调理解用户视角，确保开发投入与用户的期望和需求对齐。你大概见过用户故事被用在产品开发上——比如“你在做一个面向客户的产品”。但我们认为，用户故事同样适用于其他场合，包括内部工具和平台。和面向客户的产品一样，这些领域也有用户。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

At PixelCurl, April recognized that user stories aren’t just for customer-facing features. To address the mentorship gap, she created a user story for an internal tool: “As a junior engineer in StudioOps, I want to easily find and book time with senior engineers who have expertise in specific areas, so that I can get unblocked quickly and learn from their experience.” This frames the mentorship problem as a solvable product challenge rather than an abstract cultural issue.

在 PixelCurl，April 意识到用户故事不只适用于面向客户的功能。为了弥补辅导缺位，她为一个内部工具写了一条用户故事：“作为 StudioOps 的一名初级工程师，我希望能方便地找到并预约在特定领域有专长的高级工程师，以便我快速解除阻塞、并向他们学习经验。”这把辅导问题重新框定为一个可解决的产品挑战，而不是一个抽象的文化问题。

— 原书第 123 页 —

Typically, user stories are written by product managers or product owners; though in practice, developers or others can also write them. The point is to create something that influences functionality from a user’s perspective. Some teams rely on the product owner to craft them and shape the product backlog, while others let anyone contribute. The source doesn’t really matter as much as making sure the story reflects real-life user goals.

通常，用户故事由产品经理或产品负责人撰写；但在实践中，开发者或其他人也可以写。关键在于：要产出一些从用户视角影响功能设计的东西。有些团队靠产品负责人来撰写故事、塑造产品待办清单；另一些团队则允许任何人贡献。出处其实没那么重要，重要的是确保故事反映的是真实的用户目标。

User stories often follow a known template that helps keep things straightforward. You’ve probably seen something like the format shown in Figure 6-1: as a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit].

用户故事通常遵循一个广为人知的模板，以保持简单直接。你大概见过图 6-1 所示的格式：作为[角色]，我希望[能力]，以便[收益]。

There are variations, too. Some emphasize the benefit first, like: in order to [receive benefit] as a [role], I can [goal/desire]. Others add more context (the who, when, where, what, and why), or even consider malicious scenarios with “evil user stories” so that the team thinks like a hacker—for example, “As a disgruntled employee, I want to wipe out the production database to hurt the company.”

模板也有变体。有些把收益放前面，比如：为了[获得收益]，作为[角色]，我能够[目标/愿望]。另一些会加入更多上下文（谁、何时、何地、做什么、为什么），甚至用“邪恶用户故事”来考虑恶意场景，让团队像黑客一样思考——例如：“作为一名心怀不满的员工，我想清空生产数据库，以伤害公司。”

User stories can be just a few sentences long. They’re short and easy to reason about, which helps you stay focused on user value rather than drowning in specs. For example, imagine you’re working on a software as a service (SaaS) tool and thinking about adding two-factor authentication. The user story could be:

用户故事可以只有几句话。它短小、容易想清楚，帮你专注于用户价值，而不是淹没在规格说明书里。例如，假设你在做一个软件即服务（SaaS）工具，考虑加入双因素认证。用户故事可以是：

As a registered user, I want to enable two-factor authentication using an authenticator app or via text message to secure my account with an additional verification step beyond my password.

You can see we’ve identified registered users as our audience. We’ve also made our request: develop two-factor authentication that supports an authenticator app or a text message as the second factor. Finally, we’ve identified why the user wants this feature. That’s it. It’s very simple, compact, and easy to understand. You don’t need to include implementation details in a user story; the home for those is probably a request for comment (RFC), ticket, or commit message/pull request.

你看，我们已经把注册用户确定为目标受众，也提出了诉求：开发支持验证器 App 或短信作为第二因素的双因素认证。最后，我们说明了用户为什么想要这个功能。就这样。它非常简单、紧凑、易懂。你不需要在用户故事里塞进实现细节；那些东西更适合放在一份意见征询（RFC）、工单、或提交信息/合并请求里。

— 原书第 124 页 —

Acceptance criteria. Teams use acceptance criteria to ensure a user story is truly complete. These criteria define what the product owner needs to say: “Yes, this meets our requirements.” The criteria help set boundaries around a story, making it clear when the work is done. Some teams like the given-when-then format (which can be expressed as preconditions, actions, and results) for acceptance tests. We can see this in the two-factor authentication acceptance criteria for our prior user story. Using the given-when-then acceptance criteria, this would look as follows:

验收标准。团队用验收标准来确保一个用户故事是真正“完成”的。这些标准定义了产品负责人需要说出的那句话：“是的，这满足了我们的需求。”标准帮一个故事划定边界，清楚地表明工作何时算做完。有些团队喜欢用“给定—当—那么”（Given-When-Then）格式（也可以表述为前置条件、动作、结果）来写验收测试。我们可以在前述双因素认证用户故事的验收标准里看到这一点。用 Given-When-Then 的验收标准写出来，大致是这样：

Given

给定

The user is registered, logged in, and on the account security settings page.

用户已注册、已登录，并位于账户安全设置页面。

When

当

They select the option to enable two-factor authentication and choose “Use authenticator app.”

用户选择开启双因素认证的选项，并选择“使用验证器 App”。

Then

那么

Two-factor authentication should be successfully enabled.

双因素认证应被成功开启。

Instead of this framework, others just use a list of items, but the key is that every piece of acceptance criteria must be met.

也有团队不用这个框架，而是直接列一张清单；但关键在于：每一条验收标准都必须被满足。

A Start, Not a Solution

是起点，不是解决方案

That said, user stories aren’t perfect. Firstly, their simplicity means that they don’t scale well. I’ve seen plenty of teams meet a block when their user stories start multiplying like rabbits. It’s like trying to juggle while riding a unicycle; you’re managing an ever-growing pile of stories while personal opinions and biases keep you off balance. And let’s be honest, we’ve all been there with those deceptively simple user stories that turn out to have more gaps than Swiss cheese. By design, stories are open to interpretation and usually don’t spell out every last detail. They’re conversation starters, not contracts.

话虽如此，用户故事并不完美。首先，它的简洁意味着它扩展性不好。我见过不少团队，当用户故事开始像兔子一样繁衍时，就彻底卡住了。这就像骑独轮车还同时玩杂耍：你一边要管着那堆越堆越高的故事，一边还要被个人观点和偏见搅得失去平衡。说实话，那种看似简单、实则漏洞比瑞士奶酪还多的用户故事，我们谁都见过。按设计，故事本来就留有解释空间，通常不会把每个细节都写死。它们是对话的起点，不是合同。

To manage this complexity, many teams group stories into bigger chunks. Large collections of stories that focus on a common goal are generally called “epics.” Multiple epics, or large groups of related stories, can form “themes,” and in some scaling frameworks, groups of themes or epics might roll up into “initiatives” or “programs.” Agile management tools encourage you to think of work hierarchically: user stories roll up into epics, epics roll up into initiatives, and so on. But remember, these terms vary and can mean different things depending on who you talk to. There’s no universal rule—just what works for you and your team.

为了管理这种复杂性，许多团队把故事归集成更大的块。围绕一个共同目标的一大批故事，通常称为“史诗”（epic）。多个史诗、或一大组相关故事，可以组成“主题”（theme）；在某些扩展框架里，一组组主题或史诗还会进一步汇总为“举措”（initiative）或“项目集”（program）。敏捷管理工具鼓励你以层级方式看待工作：用户故事上卷为史诗，史诗上卷为举措，依此类推。但请记住，这些术语五花八门，跟不同的人聊，含义可能都不一样。没有普适规则——只有什么对你和团队管用。

Nonfunctional requirements, like performance or security standards, can also be overlooked. Sometimes, technical complexity doesn’t neatly map to a single story focused on user-facing value. You might need “technical-only,” “architecture-only,” or “infrastructure-only” stories.

非功能性需求，比如性能或安全标准，也可能被忽略。有时候，技术上的复杂之处，并不能干净地对应到某一条聚焦于用户可见价值的故事上。你可能需要“纯技术”、“纯架构”或“纯基础设施”的故事。

— 原书第 125 页 —

The real headache comes when your project needs to change direction quickly. Those carefully structured user stories can start feeling too restrictive—like concrete shoes when you need to dance quickly—and before you know it, you’re so focused on checking boxes that you might miss the next big opportunity coming around the corner. It’s a bit like being so focused on following your GPS that you miss the amazing shortcut the locals all know about.

真正让人头疼的，是项目需要快速转向的时候。那些精心结构化的用户故事会开始显得过于束缚——就像你想快步跳舞时却穿着一双水泥鞋——不知不觉间，你只顾着打勾，可能会错过下一个拐个弯就撞上的大机会。这有点像：你太专注于跟着导航走，结果错过了本地人都知道的那条绝好的近路。

Despite their limitations, we still rely on user stories because they emphasize the right things: user value, early delivery of workable features, and continuous improvement. Of course, as a project grows more complex or needs to pivot quickly, you will find yourself juggling a growing number of stories and needing help to keep them all aligned. At this stage, you can start to mix and match from other established frameworks, taking the bits that work for you now and providing a space and opportunity to grow into a larger framework as you scale.

尽管有这些局限，我们仍然依赖用户故事，因为它强调的是正确的事：用户价值、尽早交付可用功能、以及持续改进。当然，当项目变得更复杂、或需要快速转向时，你会发现自己要应付越来越多的故事，需要帮助才能让它们保持对齐。到这个阶段，你就可以开始从其他成熟框架里混搭、挑选，拿走此刻对你管用的部分，同时为日后扩展成更大的框架留出空间和机会。

Impact-versus-effort analysis

影响—工作量分析

To help mitigate the downsides of user stories, like when you’re faced with a mountain of them and need a more structured way to decide what comes first, we layer on top a prioritization framework. We like the very simple, but powerful, impact-versus-effort matrix. This framework complements user stories by introducing a method that helps you decide which stories (epics, features, tasks) to tackle next.

为了缓解用户故事的缺点——比如当你面对堆积如山的故事、需要一种更结构化的方法来决定先做哪个时——我们在其上叠加一层优先级框架。我们很喜欢那个非常简单、却很有力的“影响—工作量矩阵”。这个框架与用户故事互补：它引入一种方法，帮你决定接下来该处理哪条故事（哪个史诗、功能或任务）。

The impact-versus-effort method is straightforward:

影响—工作量方法很简单：

Impact

影响

How much potential benefit (sometimes also described as impact) does implementing this feature or completing this piece of work provide to users, customers, or the business? Does it align closely with strategic goals? Will it improve user satisfaction, increase revenue, or open new market segments? High-impact items significantly improve user experience, enable revenue growth, or solve an existing pain point. Low-impact features are often nice-to-haves, aesthetic refinements, or changes that yield minimal tangible benefit.

实现这个功能、或完成这项工作，能给用户、客户或业务带来多大的潜在收益（有时也称作影响）？它是否与战略目标高度对齐？它会提升用户满意度、增加收入、还是打开新的细分市场？高影响项会显著改善用户体验、带来收入增长，或解决一个现存痛点。低影响功能往往是“有了更好”的东西、美学上的打磨，或几乎不产生实际收益的改动。

Effort

工作量

How much time, skill, and complexity are required to implement this feature or perform this task? Is it a quick fix or a long, involved project? Will it tie up your team’s most skilled engineers for weeks, or can a single developer handle it efficiently? High-effort items might need complex architecture changes, development time, or scarce specialist expertise. Low-effort tasks are quick to implement, require minimal resources, and don’t introduce much risk.

实现这个功能、或执行这项任务，需要多少时间、技能和复杂度？它是一个快速修复，还是一个漫长而牵扯甚广的项目？它会把你团队里最资深的工程师占用好几个星期，还是一个开发者就能高效搞定？高工作量项可能需要复杂的架构改动、大量开发时间、或稀缺的专家技能。低工作量任务实现起来快、所需资源极少、也不会带来太多风险。

You can quickly see where items fall by plotting features or user stories on a two-dimensional grid, as in Figure 6-2. Impact is on one axis and effort is on the other.

你可以像图 6-2 那样，把功能或用户故事画在一个二维网格上，快速看出各项落在哪里。一个轴是影响，另一个轴是工作量。

— 原书第 126 页 —

Plotting user stories or features on a grid with impact on one axis (vertical) and effort on the other (horizontal) creates four logical quadrants. Each quadrant guides how you think about prioritizing the work.

把用户故事或功能画在一个网格上——纵轴是影响、横轴是工作量——就形成四个逻辑象限。每个象限都指引你如何思考这项工作的优先级。

1. High impact, low effort (top-left quadrant). This quadrant is the “sweet spot.” These features deliver significant benefits for minimal investment. They’re often low-hanging fruit and can quickly boost user satisfaction or unlock meaningful improvements. For example:

1. 高影响、低工作量（左上象限）。这个象限是“甜蜜点”。这些功能投入极少，却能带来显著收益。它们往往是唾手可得的果实，能快速提升用户满意度，或解锁有意义的改进。例如：

— 原书第 127 页 —

  • Adding a simple filter to a product listing’s page when users have asked for it for ages

    在产品列表页加一个用户盼望已久的简单筛选器

  • Implementing a minor UI tweak that makes navigation more intuitive, increasing user retention with just a few hours of coding

    做一个小的 UI 调整，让导航更直观，只用几小时编码就提升了用户留存

Features in this quadrant are prime candidates to tackle first, as they provide a strong return on investment with minimal drain on your team’s resources.

这个象限里的功能是最优先处理的候选，因为它们在极小消耗团队资源的同时，能带来很高的投资回报。

2. High impact, high effort (top-right quadrant). These features promise substantial benefits but come with a significant resource cost. They might still be worth doing, just not necessarily right away. For example:

2. 高影响、高工作量（右上象限）。这些功能许诺可观的收益，但伴随巨大的资源成本。它们可能仍然值得做，只是不一定非要现在做。例如：

  • Rebuilding a core component of the platform’s architecture to enable new scalability or performance benefits, which might open doors to large enterprise customers or dramatically lower operating costs in the long term, but requires several weeks of engineering time and careful planning

    重构平台架构的某个核心组件，以获得新的可扩展性或性能收益——这可能为大型企业客户打开大门、或长期大幅降低运营成本，但需要数周工程时间和周密规划

  • Introducing a brand-new product module that addresses a critical customer need but requires deep integration with multiple systems and careful testing

    引入一个全新的产品模块，解决一个关键的客户需求，但需要与多个系统深度集成并谨慎测试

Work in this quadrant is often strategic. You’ll probably break down these large initiatives into smaller steps, or time them so you can deliver incremental impact while mitigating risks. They’re important, but you must be smart about when and how to tackle them.

这个象限里的工作往往是战略性的。你很可能会把这些大举措拆成更小的步骤，或排好时间，以便在缓释风险的同时逐步交付影响。它们很重要，但你必须聪明地选择何时、以何种方式去做。

3. Low impact, low effort (bottom-left quadrant). These features are easy to implement but don’t move the needle much. They might be minor improvements that a handful of users requested or small “quality-of-life” changes that don’t significantly impact key metrics. Examples include:

3. 低影响、低工作量（左下象限）。这些功能实现起来容易，但对大局没什么推动。它们可能是少数用户提的小改进，或对关键指标影响不大的小“体验优化”。例如：

  • Changing the background color of a page or adding a minor customization option that only a few users have mentioned

    改一个页面的背景色，或加一个只有少数用户提过的小自定义选项

  • Tweaking a tooltip or copy that doesn’t alter user behavior or business outcomes but is quick to fix

    改一下提示文字或文案——既不改变用户行为，也不改变业务结果，但修起来很快

Because these tasks are low-hanging fruit in terms of effort, you may pick them up when you have a spare moment or as a quick morale booster, but don’t let them dominate your roadmap. They shouldn’t displace higher-impact work.

由于这些任务在工作量上是“低垂的果实”，你可以在有空时顺手做掉，或当作快速提振士气的小事来做，但不要让它们主导你的路线图。它们不应当挤占更高影响的工作。

4. Low impact, high effort (bottom-right quadrant). This is the “danger zone” for prioritization. These features require significant time and resources but offer little corresponding benefit. They might come from vague stakeholder requests that lack a solid

4. 低影响、高工作量（右下象限）。这是优先级排序的“危险区”。这些功能需要投入大量时间和资源，却几乎没有对应的收益。它们可能来自模糊的利益相关方请求——缺乏扎实的

— 原书第 128 页 —

business case or “pet projects” that aren’t strongly connected to user needs. Some examples might be:

业务论证；或者来自那些与用户需求关联不强的“宠物项目”。例子可能包括：

  • A complex, behind-the-scenes refactoring project that makes the codebase slightly cleaner but doesn’t impact performance or reduce maintenance costs measurably

    一个复杂的幕后重构项目，让代码库稍微干净一点，但对性能没有影响，也没有可度量地降低维护成本

  • Implementing a feature no one specifically requested, which requires intricate design and multiple development sprints but doesn’t align with strategic goals

    实现一个没人明确要求过的功能——需要复杂设计和多个开发冲刺，却与战略目标不一致

Generally, you deprioritize or avoid these features. If one keeps coming up, challenge its necessity or see if it can be reimagined in a more valuable, lower-effort form. In the sidebar, consider how much April might make use of the matrix.

一般来说，你会降低这些功能的优先级，或干脆避开。如果某个反复冒出来，就质疑它的必要性，或看看能否把它重新构想成更有价值、更省工作量的形式。在下面的侧栏里，想想 April 会在多大程度上使用这个矩阵。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

April uses this framework to prioritize her competing initiatives at PixelCurl. Creating a comprehensive onboarding program (high impact, high effort) would significantly improve new hire integration but requires weeks of development. Meanwhile, instituting weekly cross-team code reviews (high impact, low effort) can immediately start breaking down silos with minimal setup. She tackles the code reviews first while planning the onboarding program for the next quarter, demonstrating to leadership that she can deliver quick wins while working toward strategic goals.

April 用这个框架来排定 PixelCurl 各项相互竞争的举措的优先级。建立一套完善的入职培训体系（高影响、高工作量）会显著改善新人融入，但需要数周开发；与此同时，推行每周一次的跨团队代码评审（高影响、低工作量）几乎无需什么铺垫就能立刻开始打破部门墙。她先做代码评审，同时把入职培训体系规划到下一季度，向领导层展示：她既能快速交付小胜，又在朝战略目标推进。

The impact-versus-effort matrix is a lens to help you see where to invest your team’s limited time and energy. High-impact, low-effort items are usually first picks, offering quick wins. High-impact, high-effort tasks still matter but may need careful staging or breaking down into smaller, more manageable pieces. Low-impact, low-effort items can fill gaps in your schedule but shouldn’t crowd out more impactful work. Finally, low-impact, high-effort features should be rigorously questioned and often deferred or scrapped entirely.

影响—工作量矩阵是一副透镜，帮你看清该把团队有限的时间和精力投到哪里。高影响、低工作量的项通常是首选，能带来快速小胜。高影响、高工作量的任务仍然重要，但可能需要谨慎分阶段、或拆成更小、更易管理的块。低影响、低工作量的项可以用来填补日程空隙，但不应挤占更有影响的工作。最后，低影响、高工作量的功能应当被严格质疑，常常要推迟或干脆砍掉。

Understanding these four quadrants gives you a roadmap for turning a random assortment of user stories, features, and ideas into a coherent, strategic plan that balances immediate impact with long-term goals. This helps mitigate the downsides of user stories, their tendency to proliferate and become challenging to manage, by giving you a clear, visual framework to prioritize what matters most.

理解这四个象限，就等于拿到一张路线图：把一堆随机散落的用户故事、功能和想法，变成一份连贯的、战略性的计划，在短期影响与长期目标之间取得平衡。它通过给你一个清晰、可视化的框架来排序最重要的事，从而缓解用户故事的缺点——也就是它们容易泛滥、变得难以管理的倾向。

Impact-versus-effort analysis helps cut through the noise. Instead of wading through a long backlog of user stories all with seemingly equal priority, you have a tool to assess their relative worth. A story that seems promising but requires a substantial architectural overhaul (high effort) might not outrank a simpler feature that delivers immediate user benefit (low effort, high impact). Similarly, you can deprioritize those

影响—工作量分析帮你穿透噪音。面对长长的待办清单、里面的故事看起来优先级都差不多时，你有了一个评估它们相对价值的工具。一个看起来很有前途、却需要大规模架构改造（高工作量）的故事，可能排不过一个更简单、却能立刻给用户带来收益的功能（低工作量、高影响）。同样，你也可以降低那些

— 原书第 129 页 —

features that would chew up a lot of resources without moving the needle on user happiness or business objectives.

会吞噬大量资源、却对用户满意度或业务目标毫无推动的功能的优先级。

This approach does more than just help you pick what to do first; it also invites conversation. When the team sees that a particular story ranks low in impact but high in effort, it encourages exploring alternatives—maybe a simpler solution achieves a similar outcome. Or perhaps a story that initially looked low impact becomes critical as business circumstances evolve. Impact-versus-effort analysis isn’t static; it’s a framework you revisit as priorities shift and new insights emerge.

这种方法不止帮你选先做什么；它还能引发对话。当团队看到某个故事影响低、工作量却高时，会鼓励大家探索替代方案——也许一个更简单的方案能达到类似结果。又或者，一个起初看似低影响的故事，随着业务环境演变变成了关键项。影响—工作量分析不是静态的；它是一个你要反复回看的框架，随着优先级变化、新洞察出现而不断更新。

By layering the impact-versus-effort analysis over user stories, you bring more structure to your decision-making process without losing the flexibility and user-centered thinking that user stories provide. It helps you avoid getting bogged down in an ever-growing backlog, keeps you focused on delivering meaningful outcomes, and encourages iterative decision making. As a result, you can more confidently say “yes” to the work that matters and “not now” to the distractions that might otherwise dilute your team’s efforts.

通过在用户故事之上叠加影响—工作量分析，你给决策过程带来了更多结构，又不丢失用户故事所提供的灵活性和以用户为中心的思考。它帮你避免陷在不断膨胀的待办清单里，让你专注于交付有意义的结果，并鼓励迭代式决策。于是，你可以更有底气地对重要的工作说“是”，对那些本会分散团队精力的干扰说“现在不做”。

Ultimately, this pairing—user stories at the core for clarity and empathy with your users, and the impact-versus-effort analysis for pragmatic prioritization—forms a balanced toolkit. It lets you maintain agility while ensuring that the features you invest in will most likely deliver real, tangible impact in a chaotic and rapidly evolving environment.

归根结底，这个组合——以用户故事为核心来保持对用户的清晰理解与共情，以影响—工作量分析来做务实的优先级排序——构成了一套平衡的工具箱。它让你在保持敏捷的同时，确保你投入的功能在混乱、快速演变的环境中最有可能交付真实、可触摸的影响。

This framework process also scales amazingly well. It can be applied to everything from a daily to-do list, to a product build, to large-scale organization-wide planning. Finally, combining user stories and a prioritization framework leaves you with a pool of work to manage: a backlog.

这个框架流程的扩展性也极好。从每日待办清单、到一个产品的构建、再到全组织范围的大规模规划，它都能套用。最后，把用户故事和一个优先级框架结合起来，你就得到了一个待管理的工作池：待办清单（backlog）。

Exercise: The Impact-Versus-Effort Mapping Session

练习：影响—工作量映射工作坊

Practice prioritizing your current chaos using the impact-versus-effort framework.

用影响—工作量框架，练习给你眼下的混乱排优先级。

Step 1: List 10–15 items currently competing for your team’s attention (features, bugs, technical debt, team initiatives, operational tasks).

第 1 步：列出当前正在争夺你团队注意力的 10~15 项（功能、bug、技术债、团队举措、运营任务）。

Step 2: Write each as a simple user story if applicable, or a clear one-sentence description if not.

第 2 步：可行的话，把每一项写成一条简单的用户故事；不行的话，用一句清楚的话描述它。

Step 3: Plot each item on a 2 × 2 grid with impact (vertical) and effort (horizontal) axes. Use relative sizing: don’t overthink exact measurements. For each quadrant, answer:

第 3 步：把每一项画在一个 2×2 网格上，纵轴是影响、横轴是工作量。用相对量级就行：别在精确度量上过度纠结。对每个象限，回答：

  • High impact, low effort: which two to three items will you tackle this week?

    高影响、低工作量：本周你要动手做哪两三项？

  • High impact, high effort: which one needs to be broken down into smaller chunks?

    高影响、高工作量：哪一项需要拆成更小的块？

— 原书第 130 页 —

  • Low impact, low effort: which items are “Friday afternoon” tasks when you have spare cycles?

    低影响、低工作量：哪些是你有空时可以做的“周五下午”任务？

  • Low impact, high effort: which items will you officially deprioritize or remove?

    低影响、高工作量：哪些项你将正式降级或直接移除？

Step 4: Share your grid with a colleague or your team. Where do you disagree? These disagreements are valuable data about differing perspectives on impact.

第 4 步：把你的网格分享给一位同事或你的团队。你们在哪里意见不一致？这些分歧正是关于“对影响的不同看法”的宝贵数据。

Managing Backlogs Effectively

高效管理待办清单

An organized, thoughtfully curated backlog is at the heart of effective product management. But I hear you saying, “I am not a product manager; product managers manage backlogs.” Yep, it’s true that they often do. But one of the many charms of chaotic organizations, that we described in Chapter 1, is that ownership is often diffuse or unclear. Both Juan and James have found themselves managing backlogs—either with the product managers who own them or by acting as de facto product managers to fill gaps or address a lack of ownership. Knowing how to do this helps you and your team manage your work.

一份有条理、经过精心打理的待办清单，是有效产品管理的核心。但我听到你说：“我不是产品经理；待办清单是产品经理管的。”没错，他们常常确实在管。但我们在第 1 章描述过，混乱组织的诸多“魅力”之一，就是责任常常分散或模糊。Juan 和 James 都曾发现自己在管待办清单——要么和拥有它的产品经理一起管，要么事实上扮演产品经理的角色，去填补缺口、或应对责任缺位。懂得怎么管这件事，能帮你和你的团队管好自己的工作。

When your backlog accurately reflects current priorities, the team can confidently focus on the tasks that matter most. To ensure this, commit to regular review sessions that fit in with your development lifecycle—for example, weekly or biweekly if you have one- or two-week sprints. In these sessions you will reassess items and confirm if they’re still relevant and aligned with strategic objectives. These sessions help you spot outdated user stories or features that were once critical but no longer support evolving business goals. Over time, pruning these stale items keeps the backlog lean, preventing it from becoming a confusing inventory of long-forgotten ideas.

当你的待办清单准确反映当前优先级时，团队就能有信心地专注于最重要的任务。要确保这一点，就要固定地开展与你的开发生命周期相匹配的评审会——例如，如果你用一周或两周的冲刺，那就每周或每双周开一次。在这些会上，你会重新评估各项，确认它们是否仍然相关、是否仍与战略目标对齐。这些会帮你发现过时的用户故事或功能——那些曾经关键、却不再支持演进中业务目标的项。长此以往，修剪这些陈旧项能让待办清单保持精简，避免它变成一堆被遗忘已久、令人困惑的想法仓库。

We prefer to prune (delete) stale items, keeping the following in mind:

我们倾向于修剪（删除）陈旧项，并牢记以下两点：

  • You already have more work to do than capacity to work on it.

    你要做的工作，本来就已经超出你的产能。

  • If it’s important, it will come up again.

    如果它真的重要，它还会再冒出来。

But if you’re concerned about pruning too aggressively—as not everyone can be a ruthless pruner—then introduce an “icebox” or “ideas” category to maintain clarity. Instead of cluttering your active queue with suggestions that lack immediate impact, park them in the icebox. This is a space for those intriguing concepts that might be useful in a different market phase, a later product iteration, or after specific dependencies are resolved. By stashing potential work here, you preserve good ideas for future exploration without burdening the current workflow.

但如果你担心修剪得太狠——毕竟不是每个人都能做一个毫不留情的修剪者——那就引入一个“冷藏箱”或“想法库”分类来保持清晰。别把那些缺乏即时影响的建议堆在活跃队列里，而是把它们停进冷藏箱。这个空间留给那些有意思的构想：它们也许在另一个市场阶段、下一次产品迭代、或某些依赖被解决之后会派上用场。把潜在工作存放在这里，你就为未来的探索保留了好点子，又不给当前的工作流添负担。

Above all, don’t maintain the backlog alone. Implement collaborative backlog grooming sessions, where product managers, developers, designers, and other stakeholders review and refine items and offer diverse perspectives and insights. This collective

最重要的是，别一个人维护待办清单。开展协作式的待办梳理会，让产品经理、开发者、设计师和其他利益相关方一起评审、打磨各项，提供多元的视角和洞察。这种集体

— 原书第 131 页 —

curation process fosters a sense of shared ownership and ensures everyone understands the “why” behind each entry.

筛选过程会培养一种共同主人翁感，并确保每个人都理解每一条目背后的“为什么”。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

April transformed PixelCurl’s backlog grooming sessions from technical-only discussions to collaborative planning meetings. She ensures Jordan and Priya, her engineering managers, actively participate in prioritizing not just features but team development initiatives. When a senior engineer suggests deprioritizing junior training in favor of a new feature, the group discusses the long-term velocity impact of under-mentored developers, making the trade-off visible to everyone.

April 把 PixelCurl 的待办梳理会从“只谈技术”的讨论，变成了协作式的规划会议。她确保自己的工程经理 Jordan 和 Priya 积极参与排优先级——不仅排功能，也排团队发展举措。当一位高级工程师提议为了一个新功能而降低初级工程师培训的优先级时，大家会一起讨论“辅导不足的开发者对长期交付速度的影响”，让这个权衡对所有人可见。

These discussions often surface nuanced details—like a hidden dependency or an unexpectedly simple workaround—that refine the feasibility and desirability of particular tasks. The result is a backlog consistently aligned with real-world constraints, customer needs, and strategic priorities, ultimately enabling the team to deliver tangible outcomes.

这些讨论常常会浮现出一些微妙的细节——比如一个隐藏的依赖、或一个出乎意料简单的变通办法——从而修正某些任务的可行性和可取性。结果就是：待办清单始终与现实约束、客户需求和战略优先级保持对齐，最终让团队能够交付切实的成果。

A Good Cadence

良好的节奏

Our experience has been that establishing a cadence of activities to manage your work and backlog is crucial. A cadence not only enforces operational management of your work but also provides structure and consistency for your team. Finding the cadence that works for you might require experimenting, trial, and testing. We usually start with Agile-style sprints.

我们的经验是：建立一套固定节奏的活动来管理工作和待办清单，至关重要。节奏不仅能强化对工作的运营管理，也能为团队提供结构感和一致性。找到适合你的节奏，可能需要试验、试错和测试。我们通常从敏捷式冲刺开始。

You’re probably familiar with sprints: short, time-boxed periods during which a team focuses on completing a set of user stories. We generally find that one-week sprints are too short, but a month is too long, especially in chaotic environments where changes in people and priorities can be frequent. So, we settle for a middle ground of two-week sprints. We then set a schedule within the sprint. Like most Agile-esque systems, we like to start sprints with planning. For example, a cadence we often use is as follows:

你大概熟悉冲刺：一段短的、有时限的周期，团队在其中专注于完成一组用户故事。我们通常觉得一周的冲刺太短，而一个月又太长——尤其是在人员和优先级频繁变动的混乱环境里。于是我们取一个中间值：两周冲刺。然后我们在冲刺内部排一个日程。和大多数类敏捷体系一样，我们喜欢以计划会开启冲刺。例如，我们常用的一种节奏是：

Week 1

第一周

On Monday, we conduct sprint planning. From Tuesday through Thursday, we hold morning standups, either in person over virtual meetings, or on Slack. On Friday, we have asynchronous standups via Slack or another shared platform.

周一开冲刺计划会。周二到周四，每天早上站会——可以面对面、可以视频会议，也可以在 Slack 上进行。周五则通过 Slack 或其他共享平台做异步站会。

Week 2

第二周

We again hold daily standups on Monday through Thursday. On Friday, we conduct demos and a retrospective on the sprint.

周一到周四再次每天站会。周五做冲刺演示和回顾会。

— 原书第 132 页 —

This cadence enables the team to plan which items from the backlog can be realistically finished. Then, the team proceeds with daily check-ins to ensure everyone remains on the same page and can quickly address impediments. At the end of the sprint, the team conducts a review to demonstrate their accomplishments and a retrospective to discuss successes, challenges, and opportunities for improvement. This cadence is just an example of a myriad of combinations of cadences that exist in the Agile world. If you find daily standups are too frequent, then try every second day. The important lesson here is to see what works for you, and then to keep testing and confirming that it continues to. If not, adjust accordingly.

这个节奏让团队能够规划待办清单里哪些项是现实中可以完成的。然后团队每天对齐，确保大家步调一致、并能快速扫除障碍。冲刺结束时，团队做一次评审来展示成果，并做一次回顾会来讨论成功之处、挑战和改进机会。这个节奏只是敏捷世界里无数种节奏组合中的一个例子。如果你觉得每天站会太频繁，那就试试隔天一次。这里最重要的一课是：找到对你管用的做法，然后持续测试、确认它一直管用；如果不管用了，就相应调整。

Approaching Estimates Wisely

明智地对待估算

In the previous section, we quickly moved over the phrase “realistically finished.” But how do we decide what work will fit into our cadence? Well, we determine this with estimates. This part of the chapter is where the classic refrain of “Danger, Will Robinson!” echoes in our heads. Estimates are both powerful and dangerous. They are an important, if imperfect, compass guiding your team toward realistic planning. Yet the quest for hyper-accurate estimates often devolves into contentious debates that waste time and erode trust.

上一节里，我们一笔带过了“现实中可以完成”这个说法。但我们怎么决定哪些工作能塞进自己的节奏里呢？靠估算。讲到这部分，我们脑子里会响起那句经典台词：“危险啊，Will Robinson！”估算既强大又危险。它是一个重要（尽管不完美）的罗盘，指引团队走向现实的规划。然而，对超精确估算的追求，往往会退化成浪费时间、侵蚀信任的激烈争论。

Instead of seeking perfection, focus on consistency. Choose a method, story points, time-based estimates, or a more whimsical approach like assigning “difficulty tokens,” and ensure everyone uses it in the same spirit. What matters most is that each team member similarly interprets the scale. Over time, these consistent standards enable you to compare tasks with reasonable confidence, making it easier to identify what’s genuinely complex versus what just seemed tricky at first glance.

与其追求完美，不如追求一致性。选一种方法——故事点、基于时间的估算，或者更异想天开的“难度代币”之类——并确保每个人都按同样的精神使用它。最重要的是，每个团队成员对这把尺子的理解要一致。长此以往，这套一致的标准让你能够有合理信心地比较任务，更容易分辨什么是真正复杂、什么只是乍一看显得棘手。

Avoid Bikeshedding on Estimations

别在估算上“画自行车棚”

Beware of the tendency to spend disproportionate time debating an estimate or, worse, debating the best estimation method. While agreeing on a shared framework is good, you don’t want to squander valuable energy on this secondary concern. Instead, acknowledge that any method will have its shortcomings and move forward, refining your approach as you gain more experience and data. Embrace approximation and uncertainty. Early in a project, you may accept broad estimate ranges—such as ±25%—and then narrow these ranges as tasks become clearer or you learn from past sprints. This openness to uncertainty reduces pressure on the team and sets realistic expectations for stakeholders.

当心那种倾向：花过多时间争论一个估算数字，或更糟，争论哪种估算方法最好。就一个共享框架达成一致固然好，但你不想把宝贵精力浪费在这种次要问题上。相反，要承认任何方法都有缺点，然后往前走，随着经验和数据增多再打磨方法。拥抱近似和不确定性。项目早期，你可以接受很宽的估算区间——比如 ±25%——然后随着任务变清晰、或从过去的冲刺中学习，再逐步收窄区间。这种对不确定性的开放态度，能减轻团队压力，也为利益相关方设定了现实的预期。

— 原书第 133 页 —

Above all, keep communication transparent. Say so if a feature’s timeline is uncertain due to technical complexities or unknown dependencies. Stakeholders are more likely to remain supportive when they understand that estimates are guideposts rather than guarantees. When everyone recognizes that estimates are tools for informed decision making and not ironclad promises, the team can move forward more confidently and make adjustments as and when new information emerges.

最重要的是，保持沟通透明。如果某个功能的时间线因技术复杂度或未知依赖而不确定，就直说。当利益相关方理解了“估算是路标、不是保证书”时，他们更可能继续支持你。当大家都认识到：估算是辅助知情决策的工具、而非铁板钉钉的承诺，团队就能更有信心地向前走，并在新信息出现时随时调整。

Note

提示

Chapter 10 discusses estimates in the context of measurements, metrics and, importantly, measuring velocity.

第 10 章会在度量、指标——以及重要的速度度量——的语境下讨论估算。

Balancing Different Types of Work

平衡不同类型的工作

Up until now, we’ve focused on building features or new products. A genuinely resilient development process involves more than just churning out new features. While shiny capabilities and innovative enhancements draw attention from customers and shareholders, they are only one dimension of long-term success. Behind every successful product is a delicate equilibrium: you must also allocate time to fix bugs that degrade user experience, address technical debt that inhibits future scalability, and perform routine maintenance tasks that preserve system stability.

到目前为止，我们聚焦于构建功能或新产品。但一个真正有韧性的开发过程，远不止是批量产出新功能。尽管亮眼的能力和创新的改进会吸引客户和股东的目光，它们只是长期成功的一个维度。每个成功产品背后都有一份微妙的平衡：你还必须分出时间去修那些劣化用户体验的 bug、去处理那些阻碍未来可扩展性的技术债、去做那些维持系统稳定的日常维护。

It can be helpful to imagine your product as a living ecosystem. If you focus exclusively on new feature development, then your codebase might become fragile, with performance or architectural flaws lurking beneath the surface. These flaws eventually slow everything down and threaten the product’s reliability. Conversely, if you devote too much effort to technical debt and maintenance, you risk stagnation—missing opportunities to differentiate your product and delight users with new functionality. By striking a balance, you ensure that your team’s efforts work together. Stability supports innovation, and innovation justifies the investment in ongoing caretaking.

把你的产品想象成一个活的生态系统，会很有帮助。如果你只专注于新功能开发，代码库可能会变得脆弱，性能或架构缺陷潜伏在表面之下。这些缺陷最终会拖慢一切，并威胁产品的可靠性。反过来，如果你在技术债和维护上投入过多，就有停滞的风险——错过用新功能让产品脱颖而出、让用户惊喜的机会。通过取得平衡，你能确保团队的各项努力协同一致：稳定性支撑创新，创新则为持续的照料投入提供正当理由。

A lot of people look at bugs and tech debt as separate sets of tasks, sometimes even separate backlogs. A more practical way to maintain this balance is to include all types of work—new features, technical debt reduction, bug fixes, and maintenance—in the planning and prioritization discussions and in one backlog. Treat each category as a priority in your backlog. By making all these streams visible, measurable, and subject to the same prioritization criteria, you naturally create a healthier distribution of efforts. This approach leads to a more adaptable codebase and a product that can meet user needs without succumbing to the gravitational pull of hidden issues.

很多人把 bug 和技术债看作不同的任务集，有时甚至放在不同的待办清单里。维持这种平衡的一个更务实的做法是：把所有类型的工作——新功能、技术债偿还、修 bug、维护——都纳入规划和优先级讨论，放进同一个待办清单。把每一类都当作待办清单里的一个优先级流。通过让所有这些工作流可见、可度量、并遵循同一套优先级标准，你自然会创造出更健康的精力分配。这种做法带来更具适应性的代码库，以及一个能够满足用户需求、而不被隐藏问题的引力拖垮的产品。

In the sidebar, consider how April takes advantage of this approach to a backlog.

在下面的侧栏里，想想 April 是如何利用这种待办清单方法的。

— 原书第 134 页 —

In Practice: April’s Story

实战：April 的故事

At PixelCurl, April treats “organizational debt” with the same rigor as technical debt. The lack of mentorship structure and siloed working patterns are forms of organizational debt that compound over time, slowing feature delivery just as surely as any architectural flaw. She adds these items to the team’s backlog: “Implement peer programming sessions” sits alongside “Refactor authentication service,” because both impact the team’s ability to deliver value.

在 PixelCurl，April 用对待技术债同等的严格态度对待“组织债”。辅导结构的缺失、各自为战的工作模式，都是组织债的形式，它们会随时间复利增长，拖慢功能交付的程度，丝毫不亚于任何架构缺陷。她把这些项也加进团队的待办清单：“开展结对编程活动”和“重构认证服务”并列放在一起，因为两者都影响团队交付价值的能力。

Addressing Technical Debt

处理技术债

Technical debt is a topic worth covering in its own right. Technical debt is often invisible until it’s not. It accumulates like unseen rust, quietly corroding the flexibility and efficiency of your codebase. For nonengineering stakeholders, the concept can be abstract, so it’s essential to translate it into concrete terms. Explain how certain shortcuts that saved time in the past now cause longer development cycles, complicate integrations, or create stability risks. Frame technical debt as a tax you’re continually paying, either in slower release cycles or increased defect rates. When people see how this “invisible burden” affects the bottom line and the product’s long-term health, they become more supportive of investing in its reduction.

技术债这个话题本身就值得单独讲一讲。技术债常常是看不见的——直到它藏不住为止。它像看不见的铁锈一样累积，悄悄腐蚀着代码库的灵活性和效率。对非工程背景的利益相关方来说，这个概念可能很抽象，因此必须把它翻译成具体的说法。讲清楚：过去那些省时间的捷径，如今是如何导致更长的开发周期、让集成变得复杂、或制造稳定性风险的。把技术债框定为一种你在持续缴纳的税——要么以更慢的发布周期缴纳，要么以更高的缺陷率缴纳。当人们看清这个“看不见的负担”如何影响利润和产品的长期健康时，他们会更支持投入资源去偿还它。

Quantifying technical debt helps solidify its importance. For instance, show stakeholders that resolving a piece of technical debt could cut the time needed to deliver future features by 20%, or highlight how addressing a brittle subsystem reduces the likelihood of critical outages. With metrics in hand, you can integrate technical debt reduction into your regular planning cycles, scheduling dedicated sprints or time blocks to tackle these issues. Just like new features, technical debt items should be prioritized based on their impact. So fix the most obstructive problems first, and then move on to less critical ones.

量化技术债能让它的重要性更加确凿。例如，向利益相关方展示：解决某一笔技术债，可以把未来功能的交付时间缩短 20%；或强调：处理一个脆弱的子系统，能降低关键宕机的概率。手里有了指标，你就能把偿还技术债纳入常规规划周期，安排专门的冲刺或时间段来处理这些问题。和新功能一样，技术债项也应按其影响排优先级。所以先修最碍事的问题，再处理没那么关键的。

A technique we’ve adopted from product engineering is the user story for tech debt. A lot of people keep tech debt as tickets—for example:

我们从产品工程里借来的一个技巧，是给技术债也写用户故事。很多人把技术债记成工单——例如：

“Our React pages and components are duplicative and unwieldy and need to be refactored.”

This tells you exactly the problem but nothing about why it matters and what a good outcome might look like. Instead, we could convert it into a user story:

这句话准确说出了问题，却没说它为什么重要、以及好的结果应该长什么样。我们可以把它改写成一条用户故事：

As a developer maintaining our product’s frontend, I want to refactor our duplicative and unwieldy React pages and components to make them simpler, reusable, and easier to integrate. This will help us deliver new features more quickly, reduce defects caused by tangled code, and ultimately ensure a more stable and maintainable application over time.
— 原书第 135 页 —

Add in prioritization, and now you’re a step closer to comparing the apples-to-apples value between this technical debt and a new feature and balancing your feature development with tech debt.

再加上优先级排序，你就离“把这笔技术债和一个新功能放在同一把尺子上比较价值、并在功能开发与技术债之间取得平衡”更近了一步。

Taking a proactive stance prevents technical debt from spiraling out of control. Instead of letting it accumulate until a crisis occurs, incorporate routine cleanups that make your codebase healthier. Over time, this will make your engineering effort more predictable, your product more stable, and your team more confident. By persistently paying off the debt, you will invest in your product’s future agility and resilience.

采取主动姿态，能防止技术债失控螺旋式增长。不要等它累积到危机爆发才处理，而是把例行的清理工作纳入日常，让代码库更健康。长此以往，这会让你的工程工作更可预测、产品更稳定、团队更有信心。通过持续偿还债务，你就是在为产品未来的敏捷性和韧性投资。

Exercise: The Process-Debt Audit

练习：流程债审计

Identify and articulate “organizational debt” that’s slowing your team down.

识别并讲清楚正在拖慢团队的“组织债”。

Step 1: Set a timer for 15 minutes. List every process friction point, communication breakdown, or organizational inefficiency currently affecting your team. Don’t filter; just brain dump.

第 1 步：定一个 15 分钟的计时器。列出当前正在影响你团队的每一个流程摩擦点、沟通断裂点或组织低效之处。不要筛选，只管头脑倾倒。

Step 2: Choose your top three most painful items and convert them into user stories using this format: “As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit].”

第 2 步：选出最让你痛苦的三项，用这个格式改写成用户故事：“作为[角色]，我希望[能力]，以便[收益]。”

Step 3: Add acceptance criteria for each of the three top items. For each story, identify the following:

第 3 步：为这三项各加验收标准。为每条故事，明确以下内容：

  • Current cost (hours lost per week, morale impact, delivery delays)

    当前代价（每周损失的工时、对士气的影响、交付延误）

  • Minimum viable fix (the 20% effort that gets 80% improvement)

    最小可行修复（投入 20% 努力、获得 80% 改进的那一招）

  • Success metric (how you’ll know it’s better)

    成功指标（你怎么知道它变好了）

You can then add these to your actual backlog alongside technical work. If that feels uncomfortable, ask yourself: would you tolerate the equivalent technical debt?

然后你就可以把这些项和技术工作一起加进你真实的待办清单。如果这让你觉得别扭，问问自己：你会容忍同等量级的技术债吗？

Monitoring Progress and Adjusting Priorities

监控进度并调整优先级

Maintaining a sense of direction in chaotic, fast-moving environments can be challenging. This is why regular progress tracking is indispensable. By defining clear success metrics for various categories of work, like the number of successfully shipped features in a quarter, the average resolution time for critical bugs, or the reduction in certain performance bottlenecks, you create a basis for informed decision making. These metrics act as beacons, helping you see whether your team’s current trajectory aligns with larger organizational goals.

在混乱、快速变化的环境里保持方向感，是件难事。正因如此，定期追踪进度不可或缺。通过为各类工作定义清晰的成功指标——比如一个季度成功交付的功能数、严重 bug 的平均修复时长、或某些性能瓶颈的缓解程度——你就为知情决策建立了基础。这些指标像灯塔一样，帮你看清团队当前的轨迹是否与更大的组织目标对齐。

Note

提示

We’ll talk more about metrics specifics in Chapter 10.

我们会在第 10 章更详细地讨论指标的具体内容。

Holding periodic reviews weekly, biweekly, or monthly, enables you to step back and evaluate whether the chosen priorities pay dividends. If a certain initiative isn’t yielding the expected results, it might be time to pivot. If an unforeseen opportunity arises, you might reallocate resources to seize it. This flexibility ensures you’re not locked into a static plan that doesn’t respond to reality. Instead, you can gracefully shift gears as conditions evolve, ensuring your efforts remain nimble and outcome driven.

每周、每双周或每月定期做回顾，让你能够退后一步，评估所选的优先级是否正在产生回报。如果某项举措没有带来预期结果，也许该转向了。如果出现了意料之外的机会，你也许该重新调配资源去抓住它。这种灵活性确保你不会被锁死在一份不响应现实的静态计划里。相反，你可以随环境演变从容地换挡，确保你的努力始终敏捷、以结果为导向。

This adaptive approach also reduces wasted effort. Regularly assessing performance and outcomes minimizes the risk of pouring time into initiatives that no longer make sense. Instead of discovering misalignments after weeks or months of labor, you promptly identify them and correct course. The result is a more efficient use of resources and a team that feels empowered to navigate uncertainty rather than be hindered by it.

这种自适应的做法也减少了无用功。定期评估表现和结果，能把“把时间投在已经不再有意义的举措上”的风险降到最低。你不必在忙活了几周或几个月之后才发现方向跑偏，而是能及时发现、及时纠偏。结果是：资源利用更高效，团队也感到自己被赋能去驾驭不确定性，而不是被它阻碍。

Communicating Priorities Transparently

透明地沟通优先级

Just reviewing and updating your priorities is the first step. Once you’ve done it, you need open and honest communication about the outcomes—even if the news isn’t good. We love to shout our good news, especially in chaotic environments; a win is a win. But the bad news we tend to want to mumble or send via email on a Friday afternoon at 6:00 p.m. Honest and transparent communication helps transform chaotic conditions into manageable challenges. When you share not just what you’re prioritizing but also why, you foster an environment of trust and understanding. For example, explaining that a particular feature leaped ahead in the queue because it directly addresses a top customer complaint gives context to your team and stakeholders. It shows that decisions aren’t made arbitrarily; they’re guided by a logic rooted in user feedback, business objectives, or technical constraints. The same is true of changed priorities; if you made a commitment, then transparently sharing the new situation might be painful, but nothing erodes trust faster than silently missed deadlines.

仅仅评审和更新优先级，只是第一步。做完之后，你还需要就结果进行开放、诚实的沟通——哪怕消息并不妙。我们都喜欢大声宣布好消息，尤其是在混乱环境里；赢了就是赢了。但坏消息，我们往往想含糊带过，或者挑个周五下午六点发封邮件了事。诚实透明的沟通，能把混乱的局面转化为可管理的挑战。当你不仅分享“你在优先做什么”、还分享“为什么”时，你就在培育一种信任与理解的氛围。例如，解释某个功能为什么在队列里跳到了前面——因为它直接回应了客户投诉最多的问题——就给你的团队和利益相关方提供了背景。这表明决策不是随意做出的，而是由根植于用户反馈、业务目标或技术约束的逻辑所引导的。优先级变了也是一样：如果你做过承诺，透明地分享新情况也许会令人难堪，但没有什么比“默默错过截止日期”更快地侵蚀信任了。
